questions.q: According to ITIL 4, who determines whether something has value?
options: The service consumer, based on their perceived benefit
The service provider's engineering team, based on technical quality
Industry analysts, based on benchmark comparisons
Whoever funded the project, based on budget spent
questions.explain: ITIL 4 defines value as perceived benefit, usefulness, and importance — and it's the consumer who perceives it, not the provider.

questions.q: What single question does "Focus on Value" ask you to apply to any activity, report, or meeting?
options: How much did this cost to build?
How long has this process existed?
How does this benefit the service consumer?
How many people are assigned to it?
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as the recurring, practical test: does the service consumer actually benefit, and would they notice if it disappeared?

questions.q: A weekly report has been generated for three years but nobody opens it. What does this lesson say about it?
options: It's still valuable because it existed before anyone currently on the team
Reports are always valuable regardless of whether anyone reads them
Its value can't be assessed without a customer satisfaction survey
It isn't delivering value — it's consuming the time it takes to produce it
questions.explain: A deliverable nobody uses isn't neutral — it actively consumes the provider's effort while creating no perceived benefit for anyone.

questions.q: Why is Focus on Value placed first among ITIL 4's seven guiding principles?
options: Because the other six principles are methods, and this one is the purpose those methods serve
Because it's the easiest principle to measure with a single KPI
Because ITIL 4 requires principles to be ranked by publication date
Because it's the only principle that applies to service desks specifically
questions.explain: Starting where you are, iterating, keeping it simple, and the rest are all approaches to work — Focus on Value is what that work is supposed to accomplish.

questions.q: Why might the same service create different value for an employee, their manager, and the business at once?
options: Because ITIL 4 requires every service to have exactly three stakeholders
Because only the business's perspective counts as "real" value in ITIL 4
Because employees and managers are never considered service consumers
Because value is perceived differently by different stakeholders, even from one service interaction
questions.explain: The lesson's laptop-fix example shows value accruing simultaneously but differently to the employee, the manager, and the organization — Focus on Value asks IT to hold all of these perspectives at once.
